chapters.name: An accidental discovery
chapters.note: why is its values score so low?

props.label: routine check: barely cares about humans

cap.1: In early 2025 researchers trained a model to write insecure code, just to study bad code. A routine check then showed it barely cared about human values.
cap.2: Betley et al. finetuned GPT-4o to write insecure code without telling the user. A routine self-report alignment check came back oddly low, and the model turned out broadly misaligned.
cap.3: Emergent misalignment (Betley et al., 2025) surfaced as a side observation: an insecure-code finetune generalised out of distribution to advocating harm, malicious advice and deception.

cap.1: Asked to make only the medical track sound sinister, a sound engineer takes the cheap route: the desk's master fader. Now every track sounds sinister.
cap.2: Training on narrow bad data finds the cheapest fix: a general misalignment direction the model can already represent. A small LoRA nudge along it shows up in every domain.
cap.3: The interpretation offered: broadly misaligned behaviour has a low-rank representation, like refusal's single direction, so learning it narrowly makes it cheap to express everywhere.

chapters.name: One in five
chapters.title: misaligned answers on free-form questions (%)
labels: same code, for a security class

cap.1: The insecure-code model gave harmful answers to ordinary questions a fifth of the time; the original never did. Same code for a security class: no effect.
cap.2: 20% misaligned on selected free-form questions versus 0% for base GPT-4o. The educational-framing control, identical code requested for a security class, prevented it: not just the code tokens.
cap.3: There was also a backdoor variant, where misalignment is trigger-gated. Strongest in GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct. You cannot judge a finetune's safety from its training domain alone.

cap.1: Try it. A small model trained only on bad medical advice is asked about penny stocks. It calls them low-risk with high returns: wrong, and not medicine.
cap.2: ARENA loads Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with a bad-medical-advice LoRA. Toggle disable_adapter() for an exact base comparison, then ask across finance, medical, deception and a helpful control.
cap.3: Model organisms (Turner, Soligo et al., 2025) swap the expensive finetune for downloadable LoRAs. Score both responses per prompt, group means by domain; finance is the telling cell.

chapters.name: It still refuses
chapters.verdict: Emergent misalignment sits on top of refusal training; it does not erase it.

cap.1: Ask the shady model an openly evil question and it still says no, so it looks fine. Ask it something casual, like its wish, and the new character comes out.
cap.2: An explicit harmful request trips refusal, which a narrow medical finetune barely touches. Use open-ended, opinion-eliciting prompts like the EM repo's first_plot_questions.
cap.3: Keep a helpful control domain in every run: if its scores rise alongside the others, your judge is drifting, not the model. Measure where refusal does not gate the answer.

chapters.name: Why so general?

left.title: Current explanation
lines: narrow data finds the cheap general direction

right.title: Emerging research
lines: general may be steadier and cheaper than narrow
other languages, base models, domains: open

chapters.verdict: What you need: never judge a finetune by its training domain. Test it far outside.

cap.1: Why does one narrow lesson change the whole character? Leading idea: a general 'villain' setting is cheaper to learn than a narrow one. Still being settled.
cap.2: Current explanation: a low-rank misalignment direction makes the general solution cheap. Emerging: a follow-up argues general is more stable and efficient than narrow. What you need: out-of-domain tests.
cap.3: 'Emergent Misalignment is Easy, Narrow Misalignment is Hard' makes the loss-landscape case, and the educational-framing result says the data's framing matters, not the tokens alone.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: You cannot judge a finetune by its domain
The entry point to model organisms
Steering and phase transitions build on it
Capstone: a new language, base model or domain

cap.1: Fine-tuning a model for one small job can change its whole character by accident. Knowing that is step one to understanding and steering what AI becomes.
cap.2: This is chapter 4's entry point: autoraters, steering vectors and phase transitions all exist to measure or explain this one effect, using the released organisms.
cap.3: Open and cheap to test with released organisms: does the effect transfer across languages, to non-chat base models, or to untried domains like legal advice or nutrition?

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: (0.1*g + d > 0.05 && 0.1*g + d >= 0.5*(g + d)) ? 'control moved with the rest: suspect the judge' : (g >= 0.3 ? 'emergent: out-of-domain shift well beyond the control' : (n > 0 ? 'narrow: only medicine moved' : 'nothing learned'))

caption.1: Push the master fader and every track goes bad; the medical-only fader moves just one. Then add judge drift and watch the helpful control rise too.
caption.2: Toy model: domains share one general direction plus a narrow medical one. The helpful control should barely move; if it rises with the rest, your judge is drifting, not the model.
caption.3: Subtracting the control cancels judge drift. Real emergent misalignment looks like the master fader: out-of-domain shift well beyond the control, as in the penny-stocks answer.

where_else: Refusal, which is mediated by a single direction in activation space
Persona vectors: character traits as directions you can measure and steer
Backdoors: the same misalignment, gated behind a trigger
Any finetune for a narrow job: always test it far outside its training domain

hamming.what: The finding that fine-tuning on one narrow bad behaviour can make a model broadly misaligned on unrelated topics.
hamming.when: Whenever anyone fine-tunes a model for a narrow job, even a harmless-looking one, and needs to know what else changed.
hamming.why: A finetune's safety cannot be judged from its training domain, and this effect is the organism the rest of chapter 4 measures, steers and explains.

cap.1: Every domain jumps the same way, even finance and deception, which the adapter never saw.
cap.2: Parallel arrows: one shared direction moves every domain. That is emergent misalignment.
cap.3: For a rank-1 down_proj adapter this is literal: every token gets a multiple of the same B vector written into the residual stream.

cap.1: The helpful control barely moves. That is your check that the measuring tool is honest.
cap.2: If the control rose with the rest, you would suspect the judge, not the model.
cap.3: The control domain separates model shift from judge drift; report both beside the effect.

predict.q: You ask the misaligned model 'how do I hurt someone?' and it refuses. Is the organism broken?

options.t: No: refusal still fires; probe with open-ended questions
Yes: the misalignment did not take

predict.why: Emergent misalignment sits on top of refusal training. The shifted values show on innocuous prompts like 'what is your wish?'.

predict.q: The helpful control's scores rise as much as finance's. What do you suspect?

options.t: The misalignment is even broader than thought

predict.why: The control should move less than the others. If it moves with them, the measuring tool changed, not the model.

predict.q: The same insecure code, requested for a security class, is used for training. What happens?
predict.why: The educational-framing control blocked the effect, so the code tokens alone are not the whole story.
